title: Best Hangover Cocktails: Bloody Mary, Michelada & Better Swaps
excerpt: The classic hangover cocktails ranked: Bloody Mary, michelada, Corpse Reviver, mimosa, and Fernet. Recipes, what each really does, and virgin versions that help.
metaDescription: Bloody Mary, michelada, Corpse Reviver, or mimosa? The classic hangover cocktails ranked, with recipes and virgin versions that actually help you recover.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the best-known hangover cocktails are the Bloody Mary, the michelada, the Corpse Reviver No. 2, the mimosa, and a shot of Fernet-Branca. They're fun, they have real history, and a couple of them do contain things that help a little, like salty tomato juice and fluid. But none of them cures a hangover. The alcohol in a morning cocktail mostly postpones the crash by topping your blood alcohol back up, and you pay for that later in the day. If you want the "hangover cocktail" ritual without the debt, the best choice is a virgin version of the same drink. This guide ranks the classics, gives you recipes, explains what each one actually does to your body, and shows you how to make the alcohol-free versions that genuinely help.

**The quick rules:** If you do have a morning drink, have one, make it a low-alcohol one (a michelada or a light mimosa beats a double-spirit drink), drink a full glass of water alongside it, eat real food, and don't drive. If you've reached for a morning drink because your hands are shaking or you feel anxious and unwell until you drink, that's a sign your body is reacting to alcohol leaving it, and it's worth talking to a doctor about. For everyone else, a Virgin Mary or an alcohol-free michelada does the useful parts of the job with none of the downside.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover passes on its own, usually within a day. Get medical help **right away** (call 911 in the US) if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake or be woken, is vomiting over and over, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. Also see a doctor soon if you regularly get shakes, sweating, a racing heart, or strong anxiety the morning after drinking that only settle once you drink again. Those are withdrawal signals, and a doctor can help you deal with them safely. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## What Makes a Cocktail a "Hangover Cocktail"?

Bartenders have a whole category of drinks meant for the morning after. Old cocktail books called them "pick-me-ups," "eye-openers," "corpse revivers," or simply "the hair of the dog that bit you." Most of them share a few traits:

- **A modest amount of alcohol.** Usually one spirit, or beer or sparkling wine instead of a spirit.
- **Something salty, savory, or sour.** Tomato juice, lime, salt, Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, or bitters. These wake up a dull palate and settle a queasy stomach for some people.
- **Something cold and long.** Lots of ice, juice, beer, or soda, so the drink is mostly liquid.
- **Bitterness or spice.** Many people find bitter and spicy flavors cut through nausea.

Those traits explain why these drinks feel good the morning after. The salty, fluid-heavy base is the part doing honest work. The alcohol is the part creating a feeling that won't last.

## Why a Morning Cocktail Seems to Work (and Why It Doesn't)

To pick a hangover cocktail sensibly, it helps to understand what the alcohol in it is actually doing.

While you drink, alcohol dampens the brain's main "excitatory" signals and boosts its calming ones. Your brain adjusts to that over the evening. When the alcohol wears off the next morning, the brain is briefly left in an overstimulated state. That contributes to the jittery, anxious, light-sensitive, can't-quite-settle feeling many people get with a hangover. It's a mild version of the same rebound that, in heavy daily drinkers, becomes full alcohol withdrawal.

A morning drink puts some alcohol back into your system, so that rebound gets pushed back. For an hour or two you feel more normal. Then the new alcohol wears off too, and you're facing the same comedown, now later in the day and with more alcohol for your body to clear. That's why researchers and doctors describe "hair of the dog" as delaying a hangover rather than treating it. We go into the brain chemistry and the methanol theory in more detail in our guide to [whether hair of the dog works](/never-hungover/does-hair-of-the-dog-work).

There are a few other practical downsides to drinking in the morning:

- **Your blood alcohol may not be zero yet.** After a heavy night, many people still have alcohol in their blood the next morning. A morning cocktail stacks on top of that.
- **It slows recovery.** Your liver has to process the new alcohol before it can finish clearing the old.
- **It dries you out more.** Alcohol makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water.
- **It's not safe for driving.** Even one drink on top of a hangover can leave you impaired. Brunch cocktails and the drive home don't mix.

None of this means a single mimosa at a celebratory brunch is a disaster. It means that if your goal is to feel better, the cocktail is the least helpful part of the drink.

## The Best Hangover Cocktails, Compared

Here's how the classics stack up. "Standard drinks" uses the US definition of 14 grams of pure alcohol, roughly what's in a 12-ounce beer at 5%, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of 40% spirit. Figures are approximate for a typical home recipe; bar pours are often bigger.

| Cocktail | Base | Approx. standard drinks | What helps | What hurts | Our take |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Michelada | Light beer, lime, salt, hot sauce | About 1 | Lots of fluid, salt, mild | Still alcohol; carbonation | Gentlest classic |
| Mimosa (light pour) | Sparkling wine, orange juice | About 0.5 to 1 | Juice, fluid, small dose | Bubbles speed absorption; sugar | Fine as one drink |
| Bloody Mary | Vodka, tomato juice, spices | About 1 to 1.5 | Tomato juice, salt, potassium | Bar pours often doubled | Best food-in-a-glass option |
| Bloody Caesar | Vodka, Clamato, spices | About 1 to 1.5 | Salty, savory | Very high in sodium | Similar to a Bloody Mary |
| Fernet-Branca | Herbal bitter liqueur | About 0.6 per ounce | Bitterness may settle stomach for some | Strong spirit | A small sip, not a cure |
| Corpse Reviver No. 2 | Gin, orange liqueur, Lillet, lemon | About 1.2 | Bright and sour | All spirit, small volume, easy to repeat | Delicious, not gentle |
| Corpse Reviver No. 1 | Cognac, apple brandy, sweet vermouth | About 1.1 | Warming | All spirit, higher in congeners | The weakest choice |
| Suffering Bastard | Gin, brandy, lime, ginger beer | About 1.3 | Ginger, fluid | Two spirits, sugar | Fun, but heavy |
| Espresso martini | Vodka, coffee liqueur, espresso | About 1.3 | Caffeine perks you up | Masks how drunk you are | Skip it the morning after |

The pattern is simple. The lower the alcohol and the more the drink looks like salty, cold fluid, the better it is as a hangover drink. The more it's made of spirits in a small glass, the more it just restarts the night.

## The Bloody Mary: The Classic Hangover Cocktail

If one drink owns the "hangover cocktail" title, it's the Bloody Mary. Its origin story is disputed, but it's most often credited to Fernand Petiot, a bartender at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in the 1920s, who later worked at the St. Regis Hotel in New York, where a version was served as the "Red Snapper." Since then it's become the default brunch drink in much of the US.

### Is a Bloody Mary good for a hangover?

It's the most defensible of the classics, but the good parts are the non-alcoholic ones:

- **Tomato juice** is mostly water and contains potassium, which you can lose through extra urination and any vomiting.
- **Salt, celery salt, and Worcestershire** replace some sodium, which helps your body hold onto the fluid you drink. It's the same idea behind sipping [pickle juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/pickle-juice-for-hangover).
- **Lemon and hot sauce** wake up your taste buds, which can make it easier to start eating.
- **Garnishes** like celery, olives, and pickled beans are a tiny bit of food.

The vodka is the weak link. It adds alcohol and does nothing for recovery. There's no good evidence that a Bloody Mary cures a hangover, and the relief people feel is mostly the alcohol postponing the comedown, plus the comfort of a salty, cold drink.

### A better Bloody Mary for the morning after

Makes one drink.

- 1 oz (30 ml) vodka, or none for a Virgin Mary
- 5 oz (150 ml) tomato juice
- 1/2 oz (15 ml) fresh lemon juice
- 3 dashes Worcestershire sauce
- 2 dashes hot sauce, more to taste
- A pinch each of celery salt and black pepper
- Optional: 1 tsp prepared horseradish, a splash of pickle brine

Roll it gently between two glasses or stir with ice (shaking makes tomato juice frothy), pour over fresh ice, and garnish with celery and a lemon wedge.

Using one ounce of vodka instead of the two ounces many bars pour keeps it closer to a single drink. Dropping the vodka entirely gives you a Virgin Mary, which keeps every useful part.

### Bloody Mary variations

- **Red Snapper:** gin instead of vodka. Same effect, more herbal flavor.
- **Bloody Maria:** tequila instead of vodka. If you're curious how tequila compares on hangovers, see our [tequila hangover guide](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth).
- **Bloody Caesar:** Canada's national cocktail, created by bartender Walter Chell in Calgary in 1969. It uses Clamato (tomato juice with clam broth) and a celery-salt rim. It's savory and very salty, which is nice for a dry mouth, but it's high in sodium, so it isn't a good daily habit for anyone watching their blood pressure.
- **Bullshot:** vodka with beef bouillon or consommé, a mid-century brunch drink. It's basically salty broth with alcohol in it. The broth is the useful part.

## Is a Michelada Good for a Hangover?

A michelada is Mexican beer dressed with lime juice, salt, hot sauce, and often Worcestershire or Maggi seasoning, served over ice in a salt-rimmed glass. Some versions add tomato juice or Clamato, which pushes it toward a Bloody Mary. In Mexico it's a well-known morning-after drink, and it's the gentlest hangover cocktail on this list for one simple reason: it's built on light beer, which is mostly water.

**What helps:**

- **Lower alcohol.** A 12-ounce light Mexican lager at around 4 to 4.5% is roughly one standard drink or a bit less. That's far less than two ounces of spirit in a Bloody Mary.
- **Volume.** You get a big cold glass of fluid with salt and lime, which is pleasant on a dry mouth.
- **Electrolytes.** The salt rim and seasoning add sodium.

**What hurts:**

- **It's still alcohol.** The same postponement effect applies, just on a smaller scale.
- **Carbonation.** Fizzy drinks can make alcohol absorb a little faster for some people, and bubbles can upset an already queasy stomach.
- **Refills.** Because it's light and easy to drink, a michelada is easy to repeat, and three of them is three beers.

### How to make a michelada

Makes one drink.

- Rub a lime wedge around the rim of a tall glass and dip it in salt or Tajín.
- Add ice, the juice of one lime, 2 to 3 dashes of hot sauce, and 2 dashes of Worcestershire or Maggi.
- Top with a 12-ounce light Mexican lager, pouring slowly.
- Optional: 2 oz (60 ml) tomato juice or Clamato.

### The alcohol-free michelada

Swap the beer for a non-alcoholic lager and keep everything else the same. This is one of the best "hangover cocktails" you can make, because it keeps the cold volume, salt, and lime without adding alcohol. Most non-alcoholic beers contain 0.5% alcohol or less, which is a trivial amount for most healthy adults, though people who need to avoid alcohol completely should check the label for "0.0%." Our guides on [non-alcoholic beer and hangovers](/never-hungover/non-alcoholic-beer-hangover) and [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol) cover the details.

## The Corpse Reviver No. 2

The Corpse Reviver No. 2 is the most famous member of a family of morning-after drinks. It appears in Harry Craddock's *The Savoy Cocktail Book* (1930), which recommends it be taken before 11 a.m. or whenever steam and energy are needed, and adds the famous warning that four of them taken in swift succession will "unrevive the corpse again." That line is the most honest thing ever written about hangover cocktails.

### The recipe

Makes one drink.

- 3/4 oz (22 ml) gin
- 3/4 oz (22 ml) orange liqueur, such as Cointreau
- 3/4 oz (22 ml) Lillet Blanc or a similar aromatized wine
- 3/4 oz (22 ml) fresh lemon juice
- An absinthe rinse (a few drops swirled in the glass and poured out)

Shake hard with ice and strain into a chilled coupe.

### Is it good for a hangover?

It's a beautiful drink: bright, sour, and refreshing. As a hangover remedy, it's a poor one. It's three alcoholic ingredients in a small glass, roughly 1.2 standard drinks, with no meaningful fluid, salt, or food. It goes down quickly, and as the Savoy book warned, it's very easy to have a second. If you love this drink, save it for a cocktail hour, not the morning after.

### The Corpse Reviver No. 1

The original version is cognac, apple brandy (such as calvados), and sweet vermouth, stirred. It's even less suited to a hangover than No. 2. It's all spirit and fortified wine, and the brown spirits it uses tend to carry more congeners. Congeners are the by-products of fermentation and aging that give dark spirits their flavor, and controlled studies have found that bourbon produces worse hangovers than vodka at the same alcohol dose. Our article on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains this in plain terms.

## Is a Mimosa Good for a Hangover?

The mimosa (sparkling wine and orange juice) is the brunch standard. It's the drink people most often order to "take the edge off," and it's worth being clear about what it does.

**What helps:**

- **It can be a small dose.** A 3-ounce pour of sparkling wine with 3 ounces of orange juice is roughly half a standard drink. That's one of the smallest alcohol doses on this list.
- **Orange juice** adds fluid, some potassium, vitamin C, and sugar. A little sugar can help if you skipped breakfast and feel shaky, though there's no good evidence that sugar itself fixes a hangover. Our guide on [sugar for a hangover](/never-hungover/sugar-for-hangover) goes into it.

**What hurts:**

- **Bubbles.** Research on mixers has found that carbonation can speed up how quickly alcohol is absorbed in some people. That means a mimosa may hit faster than its small size suggests.
- **Bottomless brunch.** The real problem with mimosas is how they're served. A "bottomless" deal can quietly turn into a whole bottle of sparkling wine over two hours, which is five standard drinks or more.
- **Acid.** Orange juice and sparkling wine are both acidic, which can bother a stomach that's already irritated.

### The better mimosa

If you want one, make it a "light mimosa" in a big glass: one part sparkling wine to two or three parts orange juice, over ice, with a splash of soda water. Have one, alongside water and food. Better still, try a non-alcoholic sparkling wine or just orange juice topped with soda water. You lose very little of the experience.

### Bellinis and other brunch spritzes

The same logic applies to a Bellini (peach purée and Prosecco), a Kir Royale, or an Aperol spritz. Spritzes are actually some of the lighter options, because they're built on wine or a low-alcohol aperitif and topped with soda. But they're all still carbonated alcohol, and if Prosecco hangovers are a particular problem for you, our [Prosecco hangover guide](/never-hungover/prosecco-hangover) explains why.

## Fernet-Branca and Other Bitter "Stomach Settlers"

Fernet-Branca is a bitter Italian herbal liqueur, and it has a long reputation among bartenders as a morning-after or after-dinner "stomach settler." It's so popular in the industry that a shot of it is sometimes called the "bartender's handshake."

There's a reasonable idea behind bitter liqueurs. Bitter flavors are traditionally used to stimulate digestion, and many people find that strongly bitter or minty flavors cut through nausea. Other drinks in the same family include Underberg (a small bottle of herbal bitters popular in Germany), Jägermeister, and Italian amari like Averna or Montenegro.

The catch is that these are spirits. Fernet-Branca is around 39% alcohol, so a single ounce is a little over half a standard drink. There's no good evidence that it cures a hangover, and any settling effect on your stomach is coming from the herbs and bitterness, not the alcohol.

**A better swap:** a few dashes of aromatic bitters in a tall glass of soda water with lime. Bitters contain a small amount of alcohol, but a few dashes adds up to very little. Many bars will make this for you, and it's a well-known bartender trick for an unsettled stomach. Fresh ginger is another good option with some actual evidence behind it for nausea, covered in our guide on [ginger for a hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover).

## Other Famous Hangover Cocktails

A few more drinks show up on every "hangover cocktail" list. Here's the honest version of each.

**The Suffering Bastard.** Created in the 1940s by bartender Joe Scialom at Shepheard's Hotel in Cairo, reportedly as a hangover cure for British officers. It's gin, brandy, lime, bitters, and ginger beer. The ginger beer and lime are pleasant on a rough stomach, but two spirits make it one of the stronger drinks here.

**The Prairie Oyster.** Not really a cocktail. The classic version is a raw egg yolk swallowed whole with Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, salt, and pepper, sometimes with tomato juice. Some versions add brandy. It's more of a dare than a remedy, and raw eggs carry a small risk of salmonella. If you want eggs after drinking, cook them. Our guide on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains why they're a reasonable breakfast. We cover the prairie oyster and other legendary remedies in [famous hangover cures](/never-hungover/famous-hangover-cures).

**The espresso martini.** Vodka, coffee liqueur, and espresso. It's popular at brunch because coffee feels like a morning thing, but caffeine on top of alcohol can mask how impaired you are, and the drink is mostly spirit. If you want coffee the morning after, have coffee. Our [coffee for a hangover](/never-hungover/coffee-for-hangover) guide covers how to do that without making dehydration or an upset stomach worse.

**The Irish coffee.** Hot coffee, Irish whiskey, sugar, and cream. Comforting, but it combines caffeine with a dark spirit, and whiskey is higher in congeners than clear spirits.

**Shandies and red beer.** A shandy (beer mixed with lemonade or citrus soda) and red beer (light beer with tomato juice, popular in parts of the American Midwest) are both lower in alcohol than the beer alone, since the mixer dilutes it. Like the michelada, they're among the gentler choices if you're going to drink at all.

## The Best Hangover Cocktails Are the Virgin Versions

Here's the practical takeaway. Almost every classic hangover cocktail has a non-alcoholic version that keeps the good parts (fluid, salt, flavor, the ritual) and drops the part that slows your recovery. These are the ones we'd actually recommend.

### 1. Virgin Mary

The Bloody Mary recipe above with no vodka. Tomato juice, lemon, Worcestershire, hot sauce, and celery salt over ice. It's salty, savory, and filling, and it's close to having a cup of cold soup.

### 2. Alcohol-free michelada

Non-alcoholic lager, lime juice, hot sauce, Worcestershire, and a salt rim. Cold, fizzy, salty, and refreshing.

### 3. Ginger-lime fizz

Grate a teaspoon of fresh ginger (or use 1/2 oz of ginger syrup), add the juice of half a lime and a pinch of salt, and top with soda water over ice. It's a simple drink that targets nausea and thirst at the same time.

### 4. Coconut water cooler

Coconut water, a squeeze of lime, a few mint leaves, and a pinch of salt over ice. Coconut water is high in potassium but fairly low in sodium, so the pinch of salt helps. Our [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) guide explains how it compares to sports drinks.

### 5. The "bartender's soda"

A tall glass of soda water with lime and a few dashes of aromatic bitters. It's what a lot of bartenders drink on their own rough mornings.

### 6. Electrolyte "margarita"

Mix a lime-flavored electrolyte powder or oral rehydration solution with cold water, add fresh lime, and serve over ice with a salt rim. It looks and tastes like a cocktail, and it's doing exactly what a hangover drink should do: putting back fluid and sodium. If you'd rather make the base yourself, see our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) recipe.

## What Cocktails Give You the Least Hangover?

Some searches for "hangover cocktails" are really asking a different question: which cocktails can I drink at night and feel least bad tomorrow? The honest answer is that the amount of alcohol matters far more than the recipe, but a few choices tilt the odds in your favor:

- **Clear spirits with soda water.** A vodka soda or gin and tonic with a single pour is easy to count and lower in congeners than dark spirits.
- **Long drinks over short ones.** A highball with lots of mixer and ice is easier to pace than a strong drink in a small glass.
- **Spritzes and lower-alcohol aperitifs.** Wine or a low-alcohol bitter topped with soda.
- **Drinks you can count.** One cocktail with one measured pour of spirit, instead of punches, pitchers, or drinks with several spirits.

Avoid the drinks that sneak in more alcohol than you think, like the Long Island iced tea, punches, and frozen drinks. Our ranking of the [worst cocktails for hangovers](/never-hungover/worst-cocktails-for-hangovers) explains why each one causes trouble.

## How to Order a Brunch Cocktail Without Wrecking Your Day

If you're going to brunch and want to join in, these habits keep a morning drink from turning into a lost afternoon:

1. **Eat first, or at least at the same time.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed.
2. **Pick the lightest version.** A michelada, a light mimosa, or a single-pour Bloody Mary.
3. **Ask for a single pour.** Many bar Bloody Marys contain two ounces of spirit or more. You can ask for one ounce.
4. **Pair every drink with a glass of water.** This is the most reliable way to slow down.
5. **Stop at one if you're already hungover.** One drink postpones the comedown a bit. Several drinks starts a new night.
6. **Don't drive.** Not after a morning drink, and often not after a heavy night even without one.

## When a Morning Drink Is a Warning Sign

Most people who order a Bloody Mary at brunch do it for fun or tradition. That's fine. But it's worth knowing the difference between a hangover and alcohol withdrawal, because the "hair of the dog" can hide a real problem.

A hangover is uncomfortable, but you don't *need* a drink to feel better. You need time, water, food, and sleep. Withdrawal is different. It happens when your body has adapted to regular, heavy drinking, and it can cause shaking hands, sweating, a racing heart, nausea, strong anxiety, and trouble sleeping within hours of your last drink. If a morning drink reliably makes those symptoms go away, that's a sign your body has become dependent on alcohol.

That's worth taking seriously, and it's nothing to be embarrassed about. Talk to a doctor. Stopping suddenly after a long stretch of heavy daily drinking can be dangerous, and severe withdrawal can cause seizures or confusion, so it's safer to get medical advice before you cut back. If someone has a seizure, sees or hears things that aren't there, or becomes very confused after stopping drinking, call 911.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover

No cocktail beats the basics. If you're hungover right now, these are the steps with the best support:

- **Water and electrolytes.** Sip steadily rather than gulping. An electrolyte drink helps if you've been sick or sweated a lot. Our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares the options.
- **Food.** Something with carbohydrates and protein, like toast and eggs or a breakfast burrito, helps steady your blood sugar and your stomach. See our [best hangover breakfast](/never-hungover/best-hangover-breakfast) ideas.
- **A pain reliever, carefully.** Ibuprofen with food can help a headache, but it can irritate your stomach. Be cautious with acetaminophen (Tylenol) after heavy drinking, and read our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) first.
- **Sleep and time.** Most hangovers improve a lot by the afternoon. There's no shortcut that beats your liver finishing its job.

And next time, the best hangover cocktail is the one you didn't need. Pacing yourself, eating a proper meal before you drink, alternating drinks with water, and stopping a couple of hours before bed do more than any morning remedy. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the strongest evidence.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who enjoy cocktails also take a supplement called DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, usually taken while drinking or before bed. It's been studied mostly in animals and lab work, where it appears to affect how the brain responds to alcohol and how alcohol is broken down. Human evidence is still limited, so there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers reliably, and it doesn't change how much alcohol is in your blood or make it safe to drive. Think of it as a possible extra on top of the basics, not a replacement for drinking less.

If you want to try it, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- The classic hangover cocktails are the Bloody Mary, the michelada, the Corpse Reviver No. 2, the mimosa, and bitter liqueurs like Fernet-Branca.
- None of them cures a hangover. The alcohol in them postpones the comedown and adds to what your body has to clear.
- The useful parts are the fluid, salt, potassium, and flavor. That's why the michelada and the Bloody Mary are better choices than spirit-only drinks like the Corpse Reviver.
- If you do have one, have one, make it light, drink water with it, eat, and don't drive.
- The virgin versions, like a Virgin Mary, an alcohol-free michelada, or a ginger-lime fizz, keep the benefits without the downside.
- If you regularly need a morning drink to stop shaking or anxiety, talk to a doctor. That's a sign of withdrawal, not a hangover.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best cocktail for a hangover?**

The most popular choice is the Bloody Mary, and the gentlest classic is the michelada, which is built on light beer with lime and salt. But no cocktail cures a hangover. The alcohol mostly postpones the comedown. The best options are the virgin versions, like a Virgin Mary or an alcohol-free michelada, which keep the useful fluid, salt, and flavor without adding more alcohol for your body to clear.

**Is a Bloody Mary good for a hangover?**

It's the most defensible of the classic hangover cocktails, but the helpful parts are the tomato juice, salt, and lemon, which add fluid, sodium, and potassium. The vodka doesn't help you recover. It tops your blood alcohol back up, which delays the hangover rather than treating it. A Virgin Mary keeps everything useful and drops the alcohol.

**Is a michelada good for a hangover?**

It's gentler than most hangover cocktails because a 12-ounce light lager is roughly one standard drink and the drink is mostly cold fluid with salt and lime. It's still alcohol, though, so it postpones rather than fixes the hangover, and it's easy to drink several. An alcohol-free michelada made with non-alcoholic beer is the better choice.

**What is a Corpse Reviver cocktail?**

The Corpse Reviver No. 2 is a classic morning-after cocktail of equal parts gin, orange liqueur, Lillet Blanc, and lemon juice with an absinthe rinse. It appears in The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), which warned that four taken in quick succession will 'unrevive the corpse again.' It's delicious but roughly 1.2 standard drinks of spirit in a small glass, so it's a poor hangover remedy.

**Is a mimosa good for a hangover?**

A light mimosa can be a small dose of alcohol, around half a standard drink, and the orange juice adds fluid and some sugar. But carbonation can make alcohol absorb faster for some people, and bottomless brunch deals make it easy to drink far more than you planned. If you have one, keep it to one and drink water with it, or use non-alcoholic sparkling wine.

**Does hair of the dog actually work?**

Not as a cure. A morning drink puts alcohol back into your system, which pushes back the rebound your brain goes through as alcohol wears off. You feel better for a while, then face the same comedown later with more alcohol to clear. If you regularly need a drink in the morning to stop shaking or anxiety, that's a sign of withdrawal and worth talking to a doctor about.

**What cocktails give you the least hangover?**

The amount of alcohol matters more than the recipe, but clear spirits with soda water, long drinks with plenty of mixer, and spritzes built on wine or low-alcohol aperitifs are easier to pace and lower in congeners. Avoid drinks that hide extra alcohol, like Long Island iced teas, punches, and frozen drinks. Alternate with water and eat a proper meal.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol the morning after drinking?**

After a heavy night, you may still have alcohol in your blood the next morning, so a morning drink stacks on top of it. It also slows your recovery and dries you out more. One light brunch drink is unlikely to harm a healthy adult, but don't drive afterward. If someone is confused, vomiting repeatedly, or hard to wake, call 911.

The best options are the virgin versions, like a Virgin Mary or an alcohol-free michelada, which keep the useful fluid, salt, and flavor without adding more alcohol for your body to clear.

faq.question: Is a Bloody Mary good for a hangover?
faq.answer: It's the most defensible of the classic hangover cocktails, but the helpful parts are the tomato juice, salt, and lemon, which add fluid, sodium, and potassium. The vodka doesn't help you recover. It tops your blood alcohol back up, which delays the hangover rather than treating it. A Virgin Mary keeps everything useful and drops the alcohol.

faq.question: Is a michelada good for a hangover?
faq.answer: It's gentler than most hangover cocktails because a 12-ounce light lager is roughly one standard drink and the drink is mostly cold fluid with salt and lime. It's still alcohol, though, so it postpones rather than fixes the hangover, and it's easy to drink several. An alcohol-free michelada made with non-alcoholic beer is the better choice.

faq.question: What is a Corpse Reviver cocktail?
faq.answer: The Corpse Reviver No. 2 is a classic morning-after cocktail of equal parts gin, orange liqueur, Lillet Blanc, and lemon juice with an absinthe rinse. It appears in The Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), which warned that four taken in quick succession will 'unrevive the corpse again.' It's delicious but roughly 1.2 standard drinks of spirit in a small glass, so it's a poor hangover remedy.

faq.question: Is a mimosa good for a hangover?
faq.answer: A light mimosa can be a small dose of alcohol, around half a standard drink, and the orange juice adds fluid and some sugar. But carbonation can make alcohol absorb faster for some people, and bottomless brunch deals make it easy to drink far more than you planned. If you have one, keep it to one and drink water with it, or use non-alcoholic sparkling wine.

faq.question: Does hair of the dog actually work?
faq.answer: Not as a cure. A morning drink puts alcohol back into your system, which pushes back the rebound your brain goes through as alcohol wears off. You feel better for a while, then face the same comedown later with more alcohol to clear. If you regularly need a drink in the morning to stop shaking or anxiety, that's a sign of withdrawal and worth talking to a doctor about.

faq.question: What cocktails give you the least hangover?
faq.answer: The amount of alcohol matters more than the recipe, but clear spirits with soda water, long drinks with plenty of mixer, and spritzes built on wine or low-alcohol aperitifs are easier to pace and lower in congeners. Avoid drinks that hide extra alcohol, like Long Island iced teas, punches, and frozen drinks. Alternate with water and eat a proper meal.

faq.question: Is it safe to drink alcohol the morning after drinking?
faq.answer: After a heavy night, you may still have alcohol in your blood the next morning, so a morning drink stacks on top of it. It also slows your recovery and dries you out more. One light brunch drink is unlikely to harm a healthy adult, but don't drive afterward. If someone is confused, vomiting repeatedly, or hard to wake, call 911.
